instructions: You are one of two independent readers for a public record that scores theories of consciousness. A prediction counts for a study if the theory's proponents fixed it before they could have known the study's result: before the study's registration, for a study registered before its data were collected; before its earliest public appearance (preprint or publication), for any other study; before the data first appeared, for a study reanalysing earlier published data. A paper that states a prediction and tests it in the same paper does not count. When the dates or the commitment are unclear, the study is not counted. Read the passages and the dates, and decide whether the earlier record, by the theory's proponents, commits the theory to the prediction as the study tests it, in time. Decide: BEFORE, NOT-BEFORE, or UNCLEAR. Answer in JSON: {"verdict": "before"|"not-before"|"unclear", "reason": "two to four plain sentences", "unsure": true|false, "unsure_why": "..."}.

core_claim.quote: Our conclusion is that Stage 3 processing is just as visually conscious as Stage 4.

source.citation: Lamme VAF. How neuroscience will change our view on consciousness. Cognitive Neuroscience 1(3):204-220, 2010 (discussion paper; commentaries and response follow on pp. 220-240)

prediction.statement: Stimuli that go unreported because attention was elsewhere (inattentional blindness, change blindness, the attentional blink) still evoke recurrent processing within visual cortex; what the reported ones add is recurrent processing that spreads further, possibly into fronto-parietal areas, and the later brain responses that go with it.

first_stated.passage: Another study (Figure 3) showed the presence of RP signals, while human subjects were in a state of inattentional blindness (IB) towards the objects inducing these signals. During IB, RP remained localized to visual areas. Objects were only reported when the signals showed more widespread interactions, possibly involving the frontoparietal network [16].

source.citation: Lamme VAF. Towards a true neural stance on consciousness. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 10(11):494-501, 2006

prediction.test_for: Unattended, unreported stimuli that were not masked still evoke signs of recurrent processing in visual cortex (figure-ground signals, early awareness-related negativity, feedback between visual areas) much like reported ones; reported ones differ mainly in later, more widespread activity.
prediction.test_against: Unattended stimuli that go unreported, without masking, show no signs of recurrent processing in visual cortex; early visual signals differ between reported and unreported stimuli as much as later ones do.

study.name: Graded seeing during the attentional blink, measured with brain waves (EEG, face targets)

source.citation: Eiserbeck A, Enge A, Rabovsky M, Abdel Rahman R. Electrophysiological chronometry of graded consciousness during the attentional blink. Cerebral Cortex 32(6):1244-1259, 2022. Preprint: Graded visual consciousness during the attentional blink, bioRxiv 2021.01.15.426792

passages.text: For example, when people fail to attend to stimuli, they will report not having seen them, as is the case in conditions like change blindness, inattentional blindness or the attentional blink.
